prompt.context: Princeton-Plainsboro Hospital is a large New Jersey single-site hospital serving a wide range of patients. The hospital's board is concerned because they have noticed a decline in the hospital's earnings from medical services even though the number of patients have remained static. The hospital has hired you to help them figure out what the problem is and come up with a strategy for increasing earnings.
prompt.question: Investigate the decline in the hospital's earnings and develop a strategy for increasing earnings.

clarifying_info.q: What types of patients does the hospital serve?
clarifying_info.a: The hospital is large and serves a very wide range of patients.

clarifying_info.q: What is the patient mix by insurance type?
clarifying_info.a: Private insurance: 50%, Public insurance (Medicare/Medicaid): 40%, Uninsured: 10%. This mix has been constant over time.
There are no other large hospital direct competitors within a 20-minute drive. There are specialty clinics and other small private practices that cater to niche patient groups.

exhibits.title: Average reimbursement per patient at Princeton-Plainsboro
exhibits.shows: A bar chart showing average reimbursement per patient (in dollars) from 2004 to 2010, broken out by three patient groups: patients with private insurance, patients with public insurance, and uninsured patients.

framework: Industry overview: understand where hospital revenues come from (private insurance, public insurance/Medicare/Medicaid, uninsured) and key cost drivers
Earnings analysis: calculate average per-patient revenue using patient mix and reimbursement data; calculate operating margin for 2004 vs 2010; identify root causes of decline
Strategic recommendation: develop options to address revenue decline and cost increases, including corporate development (M&A, JV, partnership), pricing/negotiation, and operational efficiency

questions.prompt: Given the attached chart and the patient mix (Private 50%, Public 40%, Uninsured 10%), what was the operating margin in 2004 and what is it in 2010?
questions.guidance: Strong answer calculates weighted average revenue per patient for each year, then computes margin = (Revenue - Cost) / Revenue. Candidate should note that absolute patient volume is irrelevant since we are comparing margins. Key insight: margin has fallen roughly ten-fold, driven primarily by the collapse in public insurance reimbursement rates.

math.setup: Weighted average revenue per patient = (Private reimbursement × 50%) + (Public reimbursement × 40%) + (Uninsured reimbursement × 10%). Operating margin = (Revenue - Cost) / Revenue.
math.answer: 2004 operating margin ≈ 31.6%; 2010 operating margin ≈ 3.2% — a roughly ten-fold decline.

questions.guidance: Candidate should identify multiple drivers: (1) public insurance (Medicare/Medicaid) reimbursement dropped sharply from ~$5,300 to ~$3,700 — the biggest single driver; (2) private insurance reimbursement also fell from ~$6,800 to ~$6,300; (3) uninsured reimbursement remained flat at $3,300; (4) per-patient costs rose steadily ($4,000 to $4,800). The combination of falling revenues and rising costs caused the margin collapse.

brainstorming.prompt: Given the earnings decline, what strategies would you recommend to increase the hospital's earnings?

categories.name: Revenue — pricing and payer mix
ideas: Charge more for services by partnering with other hospitals in the state when negotiating reimbursement rates
Attract more high-margin private-insurance patients via targeted advertising and marketing
Lobby the government to raise public (Medicare/Medicaid) reimbursement rates

categories.name: Revenue — corporate development
ideas: Acquire a local specialty clinic that serves private-insurance patients with high reimbursement
Enter into a joint venture with a specialty clinic, splitting profits with external specialist doctors
Partner with a specialty clinic to provide some services inside the hospital
Open new specialty offices and hire staff to enter niche high-margin specialties organically

categories.name: Cost reduction
ideas: Buy supplies at lower cost by partnering with other hospitals in the state when negotiating supplier prices
Attract lower-cost patients through selective advertising (e.g., target younger, healthier demographics rather than elderly)
Find operational efficiencies or synergies through acquisition of a clinic

categories.name: Operational / other
ideas: Explore health-reform dynamics and potential government funding shifts
Improve operational efficiency to reduce per-patient cost trajectory

recommendation: Operating margin has fallen from ~32% to ~3.2%, driven primarily by declining public insurance reimbursement rates and rising per-patient costs — immediate action is required

Pursue corporate development with a local specialty clinic serving high-reimbursement private-insurance patients (acquire, joint venture, or partner) to shift patient mix toward more profitable segments
Negotiate better reimbursement rates by forming coalitions with other state hospitals, and lobby government on public insurance rates
risks: Acquisition or JV with a specialty clinic carries integration risk and capital requirements
Selective patient targeting may raise access-to-care or reputational concerns
Government lobbying on public reimbursement is uncertain and slow-moving
Cost-cutting initiatives risk reducing care quality
next_steps: Identify and evaluate specific local specialty clinics as acquisition or JV targets
Model financial impact of shifting patient mix by 5–10 percentage points toward private insurance
Engage hospital associations to explore collective reimbursement negotiations
Conduct operational review to identify near-term cost efficiencies
